Jordan / team — quick modeling notes (SE view). I ran a local micro-bench previously on an A100-80GB with a mixed model pipeline (causal LM ~13B + lightweight reranker). Key baseline numbers (single-request end-to-end token generation):

- FP16 baseline (no KV cache warm): ~1,250 tok/s in steady-state at 1 request, p95 latency ~180ms for 420-token response on a dedicated A100 using batching = 1 per-GPU continuous stream.
- Quantized INT8 candidate (recommended for burst economics): ~1,800 tok/s with a 10-12% increase in p95 latency to ~200-205ms for same payload, but 2x effective slot density for token throughput per GPU when mixed across smaller concurrency groups.

Important operational notes: continuous small-batch streaming (we shape to 4–8 request bundles) preserves p95 better than large aggregation that hurts tail latency. For the top-10% long-form workloads (~1,200 tokens), expect p95 to stretch to ~350ms on FP16 and ~380ms on INT8 unless you tile across two GPUs (split generation) or offload reranking.

Suggested slab (12-month reservation) — conservative vs growth scenario:
- Conservative (peak +40%): 18 A100-80GB equivalents (or 9 A100 + 18 INT8-quants behind router) — target steady-state tokens/sec capacity ~22k tok/s with 30% headroom for sudden bursts.
- Growth (peak +120%): 36 A100 equivalents with a prioritized fallback to quantized variants and a burst buffer of shared on-demand capacity.

Risk: if OrbitFlux requires strict FP16 for parity, you'll lose the INT8 density and need ~1.6x more raw GPUs. Also need to instrument KV cache hit-rate (prefix reuse) — a 15% cache hit reduces slab needs materially.

I attached a quick CSV-style sketch and a proposed-slabs.xlsx for seat-of-the-pants sizing. I can run a short on-prem micro test with your anonymized 1-hour traces if you can provide a sample event window (hourly counts + token sizes).

— Ben

Thanks for the inputs — adding a few ops/architecture constraints to the recommendation: 

1) Canary plan: 2-week canary on a 10% slab (3 A100 equiv) with routing to hosted pool fallback. Canary metrics: p95 latency, tail errors, cache hit-rate, token cost per 1k. If canary passes, approve move to main slab. 
2) Autoscale policy: maintain target p95 <= 220ms by scaling additional quantized workers based on rolling 5-min token/slyrate + 95th-percentile concurrency. This lets you keep reserved capacity for baseline and shift burst to quantized on-demand workers. 
3) Observability: include token-level cost traces (per-request) and a daily regression test suite (50 canonical prompts) to detect accuracy drift when falling back to INT8.

Operational headroom recommendation: 30% committed buffer + a 20% shared on-demand buffer for undocumented spikes. For OrbitFlux numbers, that maps to Ben's conservative slab of 18 A100 equivalents with a 30% buffer as the starting point.

If you want, we can convert this into a mutual action plan and procurement-ready SOW language. I can draft suggested contract clauses for model fallback and performance SLAs (canary acceptance criteria).

— Karthik
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

2) For the canary, OrbitFlux requires a pass/fail threshold at p95 <= 220ms and no more than a 2% error increase when using INT8 on the 50 canonical prompts. Is Redwood comfortable codifying an acceptance criteria like that?
3) If we accept the conservative slab (18 A100 equiv), what is the expected time to scale to the growth slab (36 equiv) under our region (us-west)? We want to understand lead time and ramp cost.

Next steps: Marissa, can you and Jordan generate a short mutual action plan doc that details deliverables, acceptance criteria, and a suggested SOW paragraph around model fallbacks?
